newsitem.title: USA: Magellan Fund seen overweight in energy sector.
newsitem.headline: Magellan Fund seen overweight in energy sector.

text.p: Fidelity's influential Magellan Fund is increasingly focused on energy services, though that may be changing given the downward move of oil prices recently, analysts said.
Magellan said earlier this week that energy remained the top sector in its portfolio at the end of December, occupying 14.5 percent of its $55 billion in assets, up from 13.9 percent in November.
It said oil services company Schlumberger Ltd moved up to the "Top Ten Holdings" list, underscoring energy services' higher profile at Magellan.

"The feeling is that the oil services sector will continue to show very strong earnings in 1997. As earnings slow down in general, this sector should continue to do well," said Donald Dion, editor of Fidelity Independent Adviser, a newsletter that tracks Fidelity funds.
After a decade in which oil stocks were out of favor on Wall Street, energy stocks benefitted in the past year from a spike in crude oil prices.
"They were a beat up group until about a year and a half ago, so they represent good upside potential," said Jack Bowers, editor of Fidelity Monitor.
Analysts reckon oil services stocks likely made up anywhere between 20 and 30 percent of Magellan's total energy holdings at the end of 1996 based on market capitalization.

Those estimates are higher than at the end of September 1996 when Fidelity said energy -- topping its industry list as it did for much of 1996 -- made up 13.1 percent of Magellan's assets, with 16 percent of that in energy services stocks.
But since the start of the year oil prices have declined by nearly 15 percent and weaker prices are forecast, factors which may lead to a reduction in Magellan's energy exposure, some analysts said.

"About two weeks ago we got a sell signal on natgas, energy services and oil stocks," said David O'Leary, an analyst with Alpha Equity Research in Portsmouth, New Hampshire who follows Fidelity Investments.

Analysts note a so-far mild winter in the Northeastern U.S., the biggest heating oil market in the world, as well as renewed Iraqi oil exports have helped pull oil prices sharply lower in the first six weeks of 1997.
"What our work suggests is that they're pulling the plug on the whole group," O'Leary said, noting that Magellan and other Fidelity Funds were overweighted toward energy.
"The energy services group is the one they have the most overweighted, and that's the one I'm most concerned about," O'Leary said.
A Fidelity spokesman at the company's headquarters in Boston declined to comment on positions Magellan or any of its other funds holds in any particular sector or stock.

O'Leary said Magellan's 14.5 percent weighting of energy in its portfolio at the end of the year was too far above energy's 8.5 percent weighting among the top 25 companies of the Standard & Poor 500 index. He guessed 4.5 percentage points of that 14.5 percent figure was in energy services.
"That's a prescription for disaster," O'Leary said, noting the Magellan Fund has been underperforming the market for over a year now and is faced with some customers cashing out.
"I think Stanksy's moved very slowly," O'Leary said, referring to Magellan manager Robert Stansky, who was expected by many since he took over last June to slowly lower Magellan's energy position.
